title: Your own exception
summary: Make an exception class of your own, and learn checked from unchecked.

say.never: Java's exceptions are just classes, so you can write your own. A name like `OutOfPaperException` says exactly what went wrong, and the class can carry extra facts, like which printer ran out. It **extends** `Exception`, and its constructor hands the message to `Exception` with `super(message)`, so `getMessage()` works for free.
say.bit: Your own exception `extends Exception`, passes its message on with `super(message)`, and can keep extra fields.

say.never: There are two families. An exception that extends `RuntimeException` is **unchecked**: Java lets you ignore it, because it usually means a bug in the code. One that extends plain `Exception` is **checked**: Java *checks* that every method that might throw it either catches it or warns its own callers by writing `throws` after its brackets. Use a checked one for a problem that will really happen, like a scout's typo, so nobody can forget to handle it.
say.bit: `extends RuntimeException` = unchecked. `extends Exception` = checked: callers must catch it or say `throws`.

steps.title: In your lesson: Your own kind of problem

say.never: `BadLineException` means "I couldn't read this line of scouting text". It starts out as an unchecked `RuntimeException`, so change it to extend `Exception`. Then give it a `line_number_` field, so the code that catches it can say *which* line was bad.
say.bit: Make `BadLineException` extend `Exception`, call `super(message)`, and keep the line number.

steps.title: In your lesson: Checked or unchecked

say.never: `parseLine` already says `throws BadLineException`, so once the exception is checked, Java is happy. When a line isn't exactly three pieces, `parseLine` throws a `new BadLineException(...)` with a message and the `line_number` it was given.
say.bit: `parseLine` already says `throws BadLineException`; throw one for a line it can't read.
